utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case number IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. There are a few matters I just would like to share with the parties. First of all, we were informed that the Prosecution expects to need just over one session for further cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Of course, pending on the answers of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: How far I go into that next session will depend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I also was informed that the Defence and the Prosecution agreed that an earlier version of a document which was yesterday admitted into evidence, that both parties would wish that previous version to be in evidence. Therefore, I take it that we'll make it a Prosecution exhibit. Madam Registrar, 65 ter 10178, as evidence presented by the Prosecution and not objected to by the Defence, would receive number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Number P6712, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P6712 is admitted into evidence. I think I'm at a point where we already could ask the usher to escort the witness into the courtroom. The Chamber announces that its autumn non-sitting week will be the week of the 6th of October. That's a week which starts with -- the first Monday is, I think, a UN holiday, but we'll not sit the remainder of that week. Then, Mr. Weber, the Chamber has heard evidence about the role of Mr. Indjic before from other witnesses, especially the importance of his role, his function, limits to that. The Chamber wonders whether it would not be appropriate under Rule 90(H)(ii) to put to the witness what the Prosecution's case is in this respect. I leave it apart at this moment whether, at the time, with those other witnesses, whether the Defence has challenged or tested that evidence given by those witnesses about the role of the present witness. Then finally one short item. On the 18th of June, the Defence filed a 92 ter motion for Witness Bosko Gvozden. On the 7th of July, the Prosecution filed its response, not objecting to the Rule 92 ter motion provided that certain paragraphs of the witness's statement are redacted as they are related to events outside the geographic, chronological or subject matter scope of the indictment. The Defence filed a request for leave to reply on the 9th of July with its reply annexed, and the Chamber hereby grants the Defence's motion for leave to reply to the Prosecution's 92 ter response.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Indjic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, I'd like to remind you that you are still bound by the solemn declaration you have given at the beginning of your testimony, that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. Mr. Weber will now continue his cross-examination. Mr. Weber, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Indjic.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Yesterday at transcript page 25106 to page 07, you testified that the UNPROFOR headed by General Rose established without any doubt that the shelling of the public health institute had come from the Muslim positions. You testified that you'd received information about Cymbeline radar in this event from British officers that you were in contact with at the time rather than from any written report or letter from UNPROFOR. You also said: "I know that General Rose went to see Silajdzic to lodge a strong protest about what was happening." This is at transcript page 25109. Do you recall this testimony?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do with just one correction. It was not the health institute building that was fired at but the sector near that building. The intersection.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. So noted. When Judge Orie -- about this event, when Judge Orie asked you about the date of that shelling, you said at transcript page 25109, lines 10 through 13: "I know that this was in 1993 before Alija Izetbegovic left for Washington to a meeting at which the lifting of weapons embargo imposed on the Muslim side was supposed to be lifted." Mr. Indjic, this Chamber has heard the evidence of General Rose in this case and has received evidence that he served as the UNPROFOR forces -- with the UNPROFOR forces in Bosnia-Herzegovina starting from the 5th of January, 1994. I put it to you that your evidence regarding the shelling is inaccurate and not credible because General Rose was not present in Sarajevo in 1993. Do you have any comment?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do have just one comment. I am not ruling out that I made a mistake in the year because I said already at the very beginning that it's hard for me to state the dates, the months, and the years. But as for the event, I assert that I did have information regarding that incident and that's how the incident occurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, you were quite detailed in your association of why you believed it was 1993 and with General Rose. I put it, in fact, that you -- you are incorrect about this event. It did not happen as you've explained.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stand by my assertion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber, you said: "It did not happen as you have explained." That is a rather complex question. Do you mean to say it may have happened but not as you explained in 1993, or it may have happened but not before the meeting in - where was it? - in Washington took place? I mean, what's the issue?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I'm putting it to him that it didn't happen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It didn't happen at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: It's not credible evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you say such an event, that is, a shell being fired and detected by the Cymbeline system and in the area of the health institute, did not happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: In 1993 which he associates his meetings with General Rose --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: -- and all that other stuff so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. So there are two questions: Did it happen at all? And the second question is: If it happened, did it happen in 1993? These are two distinct questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Maybe I'll even just make it more simple.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, I put it to you that your recollection of this event is not reliable.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stand by the description of the event that happened and I assert that the event happened the way I described it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. We have that on the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: May I turn into private session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We turn into private session. By the way, Mr. Weber, while waiting for being in private session --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, did you receive protests about the supply of utilities to the city of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were different kinds of protests, including letters related to utilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go through some materials.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have 65 ter 30749 for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, I just wanted to see -- you to see the document, the first page, before we move on to some of its contents. This is a 27 September 1994 document from Vojislav Maksimovic of the RS Serbian City Assembly of Sarajevo to the Republika Srpska president, President Karadzic, and the RS Assembly president and prime minister. The document relates to a session that we can see in its beginning part that was held -- a session of the city assembly that was held on 16 September 1994, and at the end of this document there are requests for talks to resolve certain issues. I would like to discuss with you one of these particular issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could we please have page 4 in both versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Under item 9, the document states: "In the most recent using of Sarajevo for the purpose of raising and lowering tensions in the whole of former Bosnia-Herzegovina ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: If we could please have the next page in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: "... (cutting off of electricity, water, and gas), about 40.000 households in Serbian Sarajevo have suffered considerable financial damage. The damage is estimated at about 10 million German marks." Is it correct that the Bosnian Serb military and political leaders used the provision or deprivation of utilities to either raise or lower tensions in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: In the next paragraph the document states: "The Assembly believes that such activities should be carried out with prior consulting and informing of the political organs ..." Now, we saw this document was addressed to President Karadzic among others. I put it to you that the reason this local RS Assembly is requesting consultations with President Karadzic prior to these activities being carried out is because the raising or lowering of tensions through the use of utilities was being done by the Bosnian Serbs including the VRS. Do you have any comment?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't. I know nothing about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: How is it that the local Republika Srpska city assembly of Sarajevo is aware of Bosnian Serbs raising and lowering tensions through the provision of utilities and you, as a senior officer in the SRK, are not? Could you explain that to us? This was your zone of responsibility you dealt with every day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, Your Honour. This is a misrepresentation, a misquote. In line 17 we read that Bosnian Serbs are doing what is written here, whereas in the entire paragraph 9 we don't see who is doing it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, the Assembly -- the RS city assembly is addressing -- addressing the president of Republika Srpska to inform them prior to carrying out these activities. I tried to encapsulate that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, if you would rephrase it and perhaps then replace the word "Bosnian Serbs" by what you wanted to refer to.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, in this document, the RS city assembly of Sarajevo is addressing President Karadzic. My question to you is: How is this local RS city assembly aware that these problems should be addressed with President Karadzic and you are not aware of them as a senior officer of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps? Could you explain that to us?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can. Obviously this is a question that should be addressed to Mr. Vojislav Maksimovic who wrote this, not me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, Witness, the question was whether you can explain why you had no knowledge. That is a question we can't put to Mr. Maksimovic because you're the only one who could explain why you had no knowledge under those circumstances. Would you please answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I cannot be aware if I didn't get any information about something, if nobody informed me. This letter was addressed to President Karadzic. I don't know anything about this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The issue is that the persons in the city assembly apparently were aware and that you as a professional liaison officer were not. The question is whether you have any explanation for that. And if you say, "I've got no explanation for that," then please tell us. Or if you say, "Any information about this never reached me," tell us. But please answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, such information never reached me. I had nothing to do with utilities such as electrical power. Why there is none, if there is none.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, I put it to you that your answer there is incredible - not credible - because you did have contacts with internationals and those you received requests from related to utilities. And, in fact, you were aware that tensions were being raised and lowered in the city of Sarajevo through the provision of utilities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question now is whether you agree or whether you disagree.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's what Mr. Weber wanted to ask you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution would tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 30749 receives number P6714, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P6714 is admitted. Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, before I even received the interpretation, we will object to this for the reason that this document has nothing to do with the witness, and the witness has been explicit in saying that he is seeing the document for the first time and he knows nothing about it. He is not the right person through which to introduce this evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, the objection is denied. I think we ruled many, many times that if there is a document which is directly related to matters about which the witness testified, that that is in itself a good reason to tender it at that moment and not to tender it separately as a bar table document. The decision that P6714 is admitted therefore stands. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have 65 ter 31183 for the witness. And there is no B/C/S translation currently available for this.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: This is a UNMO sitrep dated 12 October 1992. And so you have it, I'll read out the full section. I'd like to draw you to a part of section 2 of this document. It's the daily sitrep related to the 11th to the 12th of October, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You should state who sent it to whom.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: It's a -- thank you, Your Honour. It's from UNMO Sector Sarajevo to the CMO UNPROFOR in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: In section 2 related to operations, it states in full: "I was in attendance at meeting today between Major-General Morillon and Serb and Croat representatives. Meeting concerned selection of location BiH HQ and regarding convoy corridor between Split and Sarajevo. In particular, I had discussions with the key Serb reps, Dr. Kalovic and General Gvero concerning movement of the L12," which our position would be Lima 12, "position and progress of utility repair missions. In both discussions they seemed very receptive to my concerns and I expect to achieve some progress as a result." I gave you that just for context. The next part is the one that I would like to ask you about. It says: "A related discussion concerned the difficulties we have had with their new Serb liaison officer Mr. Misa Indjic. Mr. Indjic has been obstructing progress of utility repair missions in particular and been so obviously partisan in approach, I wrote my concerns to the sector COS," which we would say stands for Chief of Staff, "who addressed them to Mr. Indjic. As a result, Mr. Indjic became sufficiently so upset to leave the PTT building today and with any luck he will be replaced." So I'm just going to stop there. The name in here says Misa Indjic. In terms of what I just read to you, do you understand that to be you?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just understood -- I just realised that it is not about me because this report is dated 12 October and it refers to a new liaison officer. And if you remember, I was the liaison officer from the establishment of the UN mission from March 1991 -- 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Second, I left the PTT building at the end of August or beginning of September. And this reference here is to October. I don't understand who misused my name to misrepresent themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go step by step here. There is reference in this document to Misa Indjic. Do you understand those references to be to you? Regardless of whether the other information you're commenting on is correct or not.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand. I am Misa Indjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's short for my name.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: All right. Do you recall an occasion where you walked out of the PTT building in October of 1992, particularly the 11th?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall because I couldn't have walked out in October because I wasn't in the PTT building then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we try to make a clear distinction. Did you intend to say you never entered the PTT building in October 1992, or do you intend to say that you didn't have an office at the PTT building in October 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I meant the first. After I left the office when I received threats that Dr. Lukic and I would be killed, I never returned to the PTT building again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You never attended any meeting in that building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To the best of my recollection, after that period I did not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Was there any occasions before that you left the PTT building where you walked out on a member of UNPROFOR or an UNMO?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you just be more specific? Do you mean that I interrupted a meeting and walked out? If that's what you mean, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: All right. Sir, I put it to you that in the view of the UNMOs, you were in fact not helpful to the resolution of matters related to utilities and in fact took a partisan approach. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The Prosecution would tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 31183 receives number P --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: There is no microphone for counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you please activate your microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thought I heard -- I don't think this document can be received because there is no English [as interpreted] translation. It can only be MFI'd pending translation into B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that Mr. Weber accepts that. Madam Registrar, the number would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 31183 receives number P6715, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P6715 is marked for identification. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Mr. Indjic, we'll come back and discuss this date a little bit later, but before continuing, is it correct that the Bosnian Serbs cut off electricity to the city of Sarajevo on 26 May 1995, that being the same date that UNMOs were taken captive by the SRK?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution then have 65 ter 19237, page 4 of the English original and page 6 of the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Mr. Indjic, coming up before you is a 4 June 1995 UNPROFOR Sarajevo weekly situation report for the week of 29 May to 4 June 1995. On the screen before you is a section that's entitled -- it's section 3, related to humanitarian and human rights issues. The section starts: "The utilities situation in Sarajevo since 26 May has been critical. On the 26 May, Bosnian Serbs cut off the electricity supplies to the city. As a result, water could not be pumped into the city." Do you now recall that the utilities were cut off on this date?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have page 7 of the English and page 9 of the B/C/S. I'm going to be referring to item 24.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Under item 24, the situation report states: "Civil Affairs has had two meetings with Lieutenant-Colonel Indjic of the BSA on the same issues of the welfare of the hostages and the grim utilities situation." Sir, according to this report, the grim utilities situation at the time was addressed with you. Do you now recall these meetings?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't. For the reason that throughout the war, there had been difficult periods when there were shortages and cut-offs of electricity, water, and gas because of events on the front lines and problems that occurred as a result of combat operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. I -- sir, based on the information we looked at today, I put to you that that's not a fully accurate statement. I acknowledge that there were occasions that certain lines were hit on certain specific times. However, I put it to you that you are failing to include the fact that Bosnian Serbs cut off the supply of utilities at times to raise and lower tensions in the city of Sarajevo. Do you have any other comment?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. We've already been through that, Your Honours. The Prosecution tenders 65 ter -- this 65 ter into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 19237 receives number P6716, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I see it's break time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Before we take that break, Witness, you earlier referred to your diary. Is that the diary you're obliged to keep as an army officer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, those were my personal notes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Have you ever shared those notes with any of the parties before this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I kept them by chance in case I decide to write a book one day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. They are contemporary notes? Or do they include contemporary notes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Those are notes that I kept contemporaneously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Are you willing to make them available? Because in your statement, I read in paragraph 28 that you're struggling with speaking decisively about dates, et cetera, et cetera, and those notes might assist in reconstructing the events in those years. Are you willing to make them available?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to think about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you tell us where you keep these notes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I kept them in my office and I had a little notebook in my bag when I was going somewhere into the field.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: My question was where do you keep them, not where you kept them.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They're in my possession in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I asked you where.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In my house in Banja Luka. My own house. In my possession.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Indjic, the Chamber is considering how to proceed in this respect, but let's first take a break. We would like to see you back in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber, how much time would you need after the break?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: It did go slower than I expected so I think I'll use more of the next section than I anticipated. I may go through, actually, the next session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. So we take a break and will resume at 5 minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber apologizes for the late point in time where we resume. And we are waiting for the witness to be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: -- to facilitate things, I'm going to be going to 65 ter 31180, e-court page 7.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Both languages?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: It's a transcript, so it's only available in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's a transcript. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may proceed, Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have 65 ter 31180, page 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Mr. Indjic, before the break we left off discussing your diary. I'd like to look at a statement that you've made with respect to this during your interview with Investigator Hogan in 2001. The question that was posed to you through the interpreter was: "... did you keep a diary of all these meetings?" Your answer was: "I took minutes of the meetings ... since it was normal that reports were written after the meetings ... and since the liaison officer is usually technical staff, he had to take minutes ... Unfortunately, most of them have been destroyed ... Since I've moved four times since the end of the war ... I moved privately, so I tried to reduce my luggage each time." That's what you told Investigator Hogan in 2001; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: At that time, you were aware that the Office of the Prosecutor was investigating events that occurred in Sarajevo between 1992 and 1995; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not know. Had I known that I did not have to attend this meeting, I wouldn't have attended it. I was misled.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. That -- that really wasn't my question. Or it's actually not clear from your answer. Were you aware that the Office of the Prosecutor was investigating events that occurred in Sarajevo during the war? It appeared to be the subject of the conversation throughout the entire interview.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not told why I was asked for this interview and what the subject was that the investigator was exploring.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, could you again focus on the question. No one asked you whether you were told about that. The simple question was whether you were aware that the Prosecutor was investigating events that occurred in Sarajevo during the war. Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not during that period, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you -- let's try to put things straight. You were not aware that the Prosecutor before this Tribunal was investigating, among other matters, the events in Sarajevo during the war? You were not aware of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I didn't even know that Barry Hogan was from the Prosecutor's Office. All I knew was that he was a Tribunal investigator but I didn't know what his function was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But what did you think they were investigating apart from events during the war, including Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't think anything. Believe me. I was told that I had to come and so I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Again, I didn't ask you what was told to you. I'm asking you whether you were aware that the Prosecutor's Office was investigating events in Sarajevo during the war. You may have read it in a newspaper, you may have heard it, you may have -- whatever source of information.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, okay. You didn't know that the Prosecutor's Office was investigating events during the war including Sarajevo. Please proceed, Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution have page 2 of this 65 ter 31180.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I'm going to read to you about the -- how the whole interview started. What was translated to you at the very outset of the interview was: "My name is Barry Hogan. I'm an investigator in the Office of the Prosecutor of the International War Crimes Tribunal in The Hague ... thank you for responding to the Prosecutor's summons today ... and you've noticed that you've been summoned as a witness, not as an accused, or rather, not as a suspect ... and the purpose of today's interview is to ask you questions about events in Sarajevo from 1991 to 1995 ... as you know, we have indicted General Stanislav Galic for the events ... the interview will be conducted in English and in Serbian ... do we have any problems understanding each other?" Your answer was: "No problems." That was what was communicated to you at the very beginning of the interview; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. This has now jogged my memory now that you have read it to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: With respect to your diary, is it correct that you misinformed Investigator Hogan that your -- most of your diary has been destroyed?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm saying the same thing that I said a little bit before. It was not a diary that I wrote regularly. It was just an occasional thing and it was destroyed. It was not something that I recorded daily. And it was not -- it was destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Is what you said to the Chamber today accurate, then, in terms of you have notes or a diary available currently in your possession in Banja Luka in your house?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's correct that I do have some personal notes, not a diary but some personal notes, in my house in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I think I've sufficiently discussed this with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I put an additional question to the witness in that respect. Now you are saying there are some notes and it was not a diary. Do you remember that you told the Chamber, this can be found on page 11, line 19: "I have the names of those women in my diary that I am keeping in Banja Luka." You called it a diary. Can you explain that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, perhaps there is a different interpretation of something. My interpretation of a diary is when you write down every day what happened, day by day by dates. This other thing is just an agenda, a notebook where I jot down things that I thought were important to me. So it was not done every day, not every event was written down, but it was just notes taken from time to time about things that I felt I shouldn't forget.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I understand that, but you used the word "diary." It's your word. You said that. And you even referred to names of women detained under the authority of the ABiH.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise if I created any confusion. I just explain. So it wasn't a diary in the sense of writing down everything that happened every day. These were just notes about important things that I wrote down in my appointment diary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Those notes are still available?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hope that I do have them. Now I can't even assert that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You told us before the break that they are in your house in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that I know where I left them at the last time, in a chest in one of the outbuildings on the -- in the attic, so I hope that they are still there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You told us you have them in your house. Just don't stop -- don't add on things that you didn't say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, I read to you your testimony in this respect. I said: "My question was where you keep them, not where you kept them. "They are in my possession in Banja Luka." Then I said: "I asked you where. "In my house in Banja Luka. My own house. In my possession." That is a clear confirmation that you're keeping it, not kept it but keeping it, in your house in Banja Luka. And the Chamber observes that you are in some respects - that is, the characterisation of the notes as a diary and in respect of where you keep them - that you are stepping back from what you told us earlier. I leave it to that. Mr. Weber, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Is it correct that you did not inform Investigator Hogan of the presence of any notes in your possession during your interview?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. I didn't feel that it was necessary. These are my private notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'll just take care of one other ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In view of your answers to the question, Mr. Indjic, the Chamber hereby issues an order that you should keep - that is, preserve - all personal notes, notebooks, diaries, whatever you call them, which contain any entries about what happened during the war. And this is an order which means that you can't get rid of them. You are not allowed to get rid of them. You should keep them. You can't give them to anyone else. And this order is not only addressed to you but it also includes an order to the public, whomever it is, not to dispose of this material. Such an order is given pursuant to Rule 54 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, and the violation of such an order is punishable, maximum penalty seven years of imprisonment if such an order is violated and/or a fine, and I think the fine is 200.000 or 100.000 euros. But -- so anyone who disposes of this material, you, anyone else, is punishable by heavy penalties. Is this clear to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it's clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you should keep them, make them available. If you say, "I'm willing to give them voluntarily," and you earlier said that you would consider that, to make them available, of course you have an opportunity still to do that, that -- which doesn't in any way change the order. But please tell us if you're willing to share it with us. If not, you're anyhow ordered to keep them at this moment, not to dispose of them. It is clear to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Mr. Indjic, I'm going to go just to another quick section in this transcript. It's completely unrelated to what we've been talking to but I just wanted to do it since we have this on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: If I could please go to transcript page 24.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The question that was interpreted to you was: "How did they know, for instance, if a request like this came: 'Stop firing because they are under fire at these UNMO observation positions,' how did they know what brigade, what unit to send the cease-fire request to?" Your answer was: "The first information on the type and direction of fire usually came from the UNMO position ... on the type and direction of fire ... because professional" soldiers "were at the positions of the military observers" -- "professional officers," sorry, "were at the positions of the military observers ... Er, the configuration of the terrain around Sarajevo also largely indicates from which direction it is possible to fire in a certain direction ... and thirdly, in direct contact between the duty operations officer and the brigade commanders, within several minutes it was ... objectively possible to find out what sector the fire was coming from ... but usually the military observers themselves, when they submitted a protest, indicated the type of fire, therefore, what it was about, whether it was artillery fire, the approximate calibre, and the direction it was coming from." Do you stand by this statement you made during your interview in 2001?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I'm all done with the transcript. I don't know if Your Honours have any follow-up questions on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I'm just going to go through a couple of quick topics to see if we can relatively finish up here. Is it correct that during the war you received approximately a hundred protest letters about sniper fire?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't be sure about the number, but I did receive a lot of protests.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could I please have the Galic transcript, not to be broadcast to the public, and -- but I believe this is open session during the testimony, but I'm requesting it not to be broadcast to the public because it does have closed session. If that's okay. Pages -- page 24, 65 ter 31178.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It now seems as if we are moving into private session. Did I understand you well that the portion you want to read to the witness is open session?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: It's my understanding it is, according to my notes here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then therefore what would not be visible on the screen - that is, a document which is -- the document is confidential but for the reasons that other portions of it are in private session or in closed session, under those circumstances, without showing the document I think you could read --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- from those portions. And then if we would have an opportunity to look at it, it not being broadcasted to the public, that would certainly assist us.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour said it much better than I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber, is this portion of the transcript which is publicly available on the internet, for example?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: If I can see the top of the date just to confirm? Yes, I see it's in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then I think we don't have any problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And even what could be seen by the public gallery is still public.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I didn't mean to cause confusion. I just was trying to be cautious. I -- I didn't -- thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: If I could have the lower portion of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: And, sir, I'm just going to be asking you to see if you can confirm your previous answers. Starting on line 20, in the Galic case you were asked: "Q. How many times in that relevant period, September 1992 to August 1994, did you receive protests alleging that snipers had shot civilians? Just an approximate number." Your answer was: "You're trying to make me say again that a sniper hit civilians. I don't remember any protests according to which snipers hit civilians. But protests to the effect that sniper fire had been opened ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: If we could have the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: "... I may have received about a hundred such protests." Do you stand by that evidence?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Did you continue to get protests about sniping through the end of the war? So from August 1994 through the end of 1995?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I received protests all the time when I was liaison officer; that means, until the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I put it to you -- and I'm going to try economise time here. This Chamber has received evidence that actually protests regarding sniping did involve civilians. So I'm going to put it to you that that part of your answer is inaccurate, that the protests did not refer to civilians. Do you have any comment on that or do you agree?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't agree with that. As I explained in my testimony also in the Galic case, any infantry fire was treated as sniper fire, which made for even more confusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: You're again not really directing my -- directly answering my questions. Are you saying -- are you still maintaining that the protests did not refer to civilians or do you agree with me that that is not accurate, that the protest letters did refer to civilians?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember that now.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. I'll move on. With respect to humanitarian convoys, is it correct that the authority to decide on the delivery of humanitarian aid through these convoys was with the VRS Main Staff and even the corps commander was not able to approve the passage of humanitarian convoys? Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was an order to approve the passage of humanitarian convoys at the level of the VRS Main Staff. Yes, I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. And this was the order that was applied with respect to humanitarian convoys? Just so it's clear to you, I'm not -- I'm not isolating it to one specific instance or order in my question. I'm asking more broadly, is it the authority -- the authority to decide on the delivery of humanitarian aid convoys rested with the VRS Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I think the previous answer answers that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. If it's clear. Thank you, Your Honour. Could the Prosecution please have 65 ter 31184. There is no B/C/S translation available.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, this is a document, though, that you were previously shown during your Karadzic testimony. Before you is an article by the Associated Press dated 26 May 1995 entitled: "French UN Platoon Surrenders to Bosnian Serbs." In paragraph 4 it reads, so the fourth from the top, it reads: "An Associated Press reporter watched Serbs take over 21 French soldiers who had been guarding Serb guns turned over to the UN at this barracks in a Serb-held suburb of Sarajevo." Do you see this portion? I just would like you to orient yourself before I continue.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I'll just read you exactly what it says, then. It says: "A Serb officer, Lt. Col. Milenko Indjic first tried to coax the French into surrender. He entered the UN quarters, unarmed, to negotiate. "The French commander said he had orders not to surrender. "Indjic then ordered military police to take positions and prepare to fire. For three minutes, automatic rifle fire targeted the building where the 21 Frenchmen were." There is then a quote in the article. "'Hold fire and watch for a white flag,' ordered Vuko Cvoro, the commanding Serb officer. "No flag appeared. Two rocket-propelled grenades hit a truck and an APC. Minutes later, the French surrendered without firing a shot." There is then a quote: "'Your politicians put you in this situation,' Indjic told the French. 'This situation has been forced upon both you and us and we have to do this to try to protect the Serb people from your bombs.'" My question to you is: Do you -- do you recall this incident, first?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember it very well and I'm proud of what was done here.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I take it from your answer, then, that you agree that this article accurately describes the events that you were involved with on the 26th of May, 1995?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It describes accurately what the journalist was able to see.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. So you acknowledge that you fired on the French areas for three minutes, and then after they didn't come out, you fired with rockets, rocket-propelled grenades; that's correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. Because it was an agreement with the French officer to provide him with an alibi in order to surrender.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Really? That's what you're saying, that this was -- that firing on the French peacekeepers was a prearranged thing? That they agreed to have rocket-propelled grenades fired at them? That -- is that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Shooting at vehicles was prearranged to provide the officer with an alibi so he could surrender.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: You agree with me that keeping -- that taking international peacekeepers as captives is not in accordance with the regulations of the VRS or, for that matter, with the -- the conventions?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not agree with you on that point because these men were no longer peacekeepers. They were persons who had lost their neutral status.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I know that is your view. Do you agree that the -- that these individuals were taken captive by the SRK after this event? I'm not talking about characterisations as to status of prisoners of war or hostage, I'm just asking you factually were they taken captive?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The Prosecution tenders this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we decide on that I have a few more questions. Mr. Indjic, you said that the journalist described accurately what he could see. He also gives a few quotes including quotes of what you would have said. Are they accurate as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are the quotes of other persons accurate as well, such as "Hold fire and watch for a white flag," which is not said by you but by someone else? Are the other quotes accurate as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They're accurate because I had told Captain Cvoro that a white flag will be hoisted and to wait for the moment when he sees the white flag.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Registrar, the number would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 31184 receives number P6717, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is marked for identification. I have no translation, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: There is a translation requested but not yet available, thank you, Your Honour. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Therefore it will be marked for identification. It is marked for identification. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honours, actually for the next document, I will have to go into private session. Sorry to be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: -- going back and forth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, I just wanted, before we conclude with -- before I conclude with my examination, I just wanted to give you an opportunity, since the Chamber has heard evidence about you throughout this case, I just wanted to let you describe your relationship with General Mladic during the war and any feelings you have about him still to this day. Could you please do that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have great esteem and respect for General Mladic as the commander and army leader. I am happy that I had the opportunity to meet a man like that in my life and that I had the luck to be under his command. Regardless of how all this ends, General Mladic has entered Serb history in the ranks of Serb heros where his rightful place is. I'm sorry that today he's here, but history marches on and one day history will show us who was right and who was wrong. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: And just to make sure I comply with my obligations here, I just want to give you the opportunity to comment on this. Many witnesses have described you as being close with General Mladic and that you had a more extensive relationship with him than what maybe your position suggested. You've been described, even, as being someone who is very trusted by the General, being his eyes and ears. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, Your Honour, I'm not sure should we have the -- I don't know what Mr. Stojanovic is going to say, but I just have some caution for it being in the presence of witness if it relates to the possible answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, of course, and I take it Mr. Stojanovic will not tell us what the possible answers would be. But do you want to object, Mr. Stojanovic? Would you then please explain what your objection is without in any way guiding the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will, Your Honour, and I will not guide the witness in any way. I just wanted to ask from whom this quotation is and which witness said something like it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber, is there --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: It is RM120, and I don't think I can say a whole lot more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stojanovic. Please, could you answer the question? Perhaps you repeat it, Mr. Weber. At least the last portion --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can answer, it's not a problem. The relationship between me and General Mladic was professional, extremely correct and professional. I am sorry that I did not have a chance to also have a different, friendly, personal relationship with General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. Based on the evidence we heard, I just want to put it to that actually that statement minimises the extent of your relationship with General Mladic. Do you have any additional comments?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not trying neither to minimise nor to maximise. I am describing objectively what our relationship was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe that complies, at least, with our Rule 90(H)(ii) obligation which is why I was asking those questions. I don't know if Your Honours would like me to ask anything else on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, there is nothing in this moment which comes to my mind but my colleagues may want to think about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: If -- if there is, I'm happy to ask whatever questions the Chamber feels appropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No further questions. Mr. Stojanovic, could you tell us how much time you would need for the re-examination of the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] During this break I'm going to try to organise myself, but I believe it will take no more than 30 minutes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that. Mr. Indjic, we'll take a break first. If you have made up your mind as to whether you are willing to give the -- the diaries or whatever you call them which you are ordered to preserve and not to dispose of, when you have made up your mind as to whether you want to give it to us, please tell us, because you earlier said you would like to think about it. We take a break. The witness can be escorted out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And we resume at quarter past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll wait for the witness to be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, are you ready to re-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I will try to do that as soon as possible -- as quickly as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Indjic, I would just like to clarify some things that arose from today's cross-examination. I would like to ask you to clarify some of these issues. You say --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this is page 28 of today's working version of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: -- that you experienced Barry Hogan's summons in such a way that you felt that you were deceived in a way. So I would like to ask you, what made you draw that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What line on page 28?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was told --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I said what line at page 28, Mr. Stojanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I don't have the line at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's maybe line 21, where the witness said: "I didn't even know that Barry Hogan was from the Prosecutor's Office." Please proceed, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was told that I had to respond to the summons and that is why I did respond. Had I known that I didn't have to do that, I wouldn't have wanted to have been in contact with Barry Hogan at all. I would have waited to be contacted by the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 32, lines 3 to 5 of today's draft version of the transcript, in response to the question where your notes were physically, notes that you mentioned, you said in one of the outbuildings in the attic in a chest. My question is: When you are giving this specific location, does this correspond to your earlier answer, that it is -- the notes are in your possession and that they are at your house?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That is correct. My house in Banja Luka. Rade Radica 230 has two buildings. They are both housing buildings.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 40, lines 10 to 11, in describing this event with the French UNPROFOR contingent in Lukavica, you mention that before fire was opened you had an agreement with the senior officer of the unit regarding their surrender. Could you please explain to the Trial Chamber how this happened and how it came about that you had an agreement with the senior officer of this French contingent of UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After I received an order from the duty officer at the corps command to place the French contingent under control and to separate them from their weaponry and their communication means, I called the French commanding officer of the unit. If you would like his name, perhaps we could move into closed session because of consideration for him and his career. I know him personally. I summoned him to my office and I told him that I had the order to disarm them and to remove them from -- or deny their access to their communications. I called him not to discuss whether this would be done or not done but to discuss the best way to do this to avoid anybody from getting hurt. We decided to enter the premises where his soldiers were together so that he could explain that to his subordinates. I did that. And this was described in the following way, that I entered the room where the French soldiers were unarmed. While he was explaining to his soldiers, one officer contacted the French battalion command through the communications devices and the French colonel ordered that the unit must not surrender. This complicated matters. So then I reached an agreement with the commanding officer of the unit, that they should be placed in the room where they were and that we would open fire at the building from outside and at their vehicles. When he would hear the firing stop, they were supposed to come out with a white flag. And then that would provide them with an alibi as to why they surrendered, because he couldn't make any other decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And did you keep to your agreement that you reached with the commanding officer of that unit?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The agreement was followed to the letter. The weapons and equipment was not taken anywhere out of that facility. It was just locked up in the room which was across from the dormitory where the French soldiers slept. The soldiers stayed in the same rooms where they were before that. There was even a bit of an absurd situation because after that, in negotiations with officers of the French battalion at the airport that were held several times at the line of separation, this French officer went to these negotiations and he had weapons, whereas I was unarmed. So in this kind of strange situation, there were even a few jokes going back and forth as to who was whose prisoner.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have any other actions? Did you take any other actions in relation to any other UNPROFOR members in that particular period and outside of the barracks in question?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now look at document P6710.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Indjic, you have the document in front of you. This is a document that you spoke about yesterday. I would just like to direct your attention to one part of the document. It's paragraph 4 -- actually, paragraph 3, if we don't count the heading, where this news agency reports, among other things, the following: "However, a Serb official at the Lukavica barracks in the Serb-held district of the city had told UNHCR that his side was prepared to see the man die rather than let the convoy pass, even though Bosnian Serb leader Radovan Karadzic personally approved the evacuation late Monday, said Kessler." My question is this. In view of your answers from yesterday regarding the authenticity and the accuracy of what was reported in this article, so this is my question: At any point during the war, could it have happened that you, as the liaison officer, would act in contravention of what the commander of the armed forces, Radovan Karadzic, personally approved, ordered, or directed?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am a professional and everything that the Supreme Commander orders I have to carry out, regardless of whether I like it or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at document P6711 in e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: This is a document that you also had the opportunity to see yesterday towards the end of the day. I would just like to ask you something about the first paragraph of the document. This is where Viktor Bezrouchenko, on the 29th of June, 1995, informs David Harland of the following: "This morning I had a meeting with Lieutenant-Colonel Indjic at Lukavica. The immediate agenda of the meeting was to arrange transfer of the Serbs and Bosnians who were stuck at the Bosnian and Serb parts of the city after closure of the Bratstvo Jedinstvo Bridge. Besides this matter we also discussed ...," and so on and so forth. My question is this: Do you recall at all any situation in late June 1995 that this transfer of Serbs and Bosnians could refer to after the Bratstvo Jedinstvo Bridge was closed?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I do remember that because that was connected to the agreement on blue roads and freedom of movement. One of those Blue Routes was the transfer of civilians across the Bratstvo Jedinstvo Bridge. At one point in time, the Muslims closed the bridge and did not permit anymore crossing so that there was the situation then that people who had crossed over to one or the other side were stuck on the side that they did not live in, so then we had the problem and had to decide and see how we could get them back to where they came from.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would now like to ask to see document P6714.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And while we're waiting, I just want to -- I ask you this: In these types of transfers, what was the role of representatives of the international community and international organisations? Meaning, this situation of transferring Bosnians and Serbs from one side to the other.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Generally speaking, UN members didn't have any responsibilities in these matters, but they would seek that the warring parties agree amongst themselves and reach some sort of agreement. And then in that case, the UN would assist in the implementation of such an agreement, also in technical terms, if transport vehicles were required and so on, then they would assist.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: So the question that would be logical next would be this: What were the duties or responsibilities of the liaison officer, yourself in this case, in such situations?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Organisational duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This is a document that you had the opportunity to see today.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like us to look at paragraph 9.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The Prosecutor put questions to you on paragraph 9. Could you please look at two lines in paragraph 9 --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On page 5 of the English version. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: It says here regarding electricity and water and gas cuts. My question is this: Do you know where Bosnia-Herzegovina received gas during the wartime period? Where did the gas lines come from?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The information that I have is that the gas came from Russia and there were always problems regarding the ever-growing debt for this gas. So I know that there were restrictions on the gas supplies because of outstanding debt.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: If you know, was it technically possible to turn off gas in such a way as to deny gas only to the federal part of Bosnia-Herzegovina, including Muslim-controlled Sarajevo, and keep the gas flowing to the Serb-controlled part?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's a technical question. I don't know the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: If you know, did it ever happen during the war that the gas supplier - that is to say, the Russian company - turned off the gas because of arrears in payments?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the answer to that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: How would you comment, if you're able to, the fact that the -- in this letter of the speaker of the assembly of the Serbian Sarajevo, Professor Vojislav Maksimovic, it says that over 40.000 Serb households in Sarajevo have been hit financially to the tune of 10 million Deutschmarks.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the answer again.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. My final question: The last set of questions from the Prosecutor related to your relationship with General Mladic. Do you believe that your relationship with General Mladic during the war went beyond the scope of the professional, the relationship between a superior and a subordinate?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe not.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you at any point in time enjoy any kind of privileged status compared to other officers of the Main Staff of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In the years of the war, did the Main Staff of the VRS have -- in its complement in Crna Rijeka also have liaison officers in charge of relations with the international community?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Were these liaison officers in Crna Rijeka physically closer to General Mladic and had more contact with him?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: By virtue of the fact that they were physically in the same location, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And in conclusion, would you agree with the assessment made by one of the witnesses that during the war you were General Mladic's eyes and ears?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Indjic, thank you for answering my questions. I have nothing further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, you announced "last question" and then another five questions followed, quite a number of them having been asked and answered previously. But I now --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I -- I really don't have anymore questions for Mr. Indjic, but just -- because the word -- the topic "Blue Routes" came up. We do have a chronology related to Blue Routes. I would just ask if the Defence could consider 65 ter 31182 and whether it be appropriate for admission just so the Chamber has a chronology of the Blue Routes available to it. With that, I have no other questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I take it that the Defence will give you an answer whether they will consider anything in this respect. Mr. Indjic, this concludes your testimony in this court. Before I thank you for coming the long way to The Hague, I would like to know whether you have made up your mind as far as sharing the -- your notes, as you are keeping them in Banja Luka, with the Chamber, whether you are willing to give them to us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I expected that you would ask me to solve this -- to decide towards the end. I did not intend to make my notes available to you originally, and I then said I needed time to think. However, now I find myself in a very embarrassing situation. I would prefer an officer of the Tribunal to accompany me on my way back from The Hague and not leave me alone for a moment until I retrieve these notes, because if a page turns out to be missing, ripped out from that diary, how I would otherwise be able to prove that it wasn't ripped out 20 years ago. And then I might be open to accusations that I was trying to conceal something. Because you have ordered me to preserve something that nobody knows how many pages it contains. I have not opened that chest in 20 years and I didn't even think of opening it before testifying in the Karadzic or Mladic cases because I thought of them as personal notes that I need not show to anybody. But I am willing to have somebody from here to accompany me until I get to Banja Luka and go to that room and then in the presence of that officer of the Tribunal I would open the chest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Therefore, I do understand that you are willing. So apart from concerns you have expressed but that you are willing to hand them over to a Tribunal official. One second, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber, you're on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know if this is something you're considering right now but just on the topic. Obviously, the Office of the Prosecutor does have investigators available in the field if there is someone needed to maintain a chain of custody or to be available to maintain -- to collect the notes, diaries, whatever is there, [indiscernible]. And then aside from that, even if that is not what the Chamber is inclined to do, we would ask that appropriate chain of custody is maintained for it and that the person who does recover it is someone who would be available to testify potentially at proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It is appreciated that you make available investigators but it is not a matter which is primarily focusing at the Prosecution. It is an additional source of information which the Chamber would like to have preserved and is -- will now be made available. The -- together with the Registry, the Chamber staff will work out a scheme by which, Witness, we try to have someone to accompany you upon arrival so as to go home and to retrieve that material and it be handed over to a Tribunal official. You will receive further instructions in that respect from the Victims and Witness Section. They'll explain to you exactly how it will work out. Meanwhile, you should refrain from any contact, any communication of whatever kind, about this part of your testimony. So usually you are free to speak to anyone after you have concluded your testimony, but here you have an extended duty not to discuss any matter in relation to your testimony with whomever, and that until you have received a message from VWS, that is, the Victims and Witness Section, that the -- this restriction does not any further reply -- applies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: A few further observations. First of all, once this material has been received the Chamber intends to make it primarily available to the parties so that they can verify whether there is -- it assists in their search for the truth. Second, hereby the Victims and Witness Section is instructed to arrange for accompanying the witness and to receive the material he hands over, and then, of course, to keep a clear record of a chain of custody on from that moment. Yes. And then I come to the point where I stopped earlier. That is, that I would like to thank you not only for coming to The Hague but also for your offer to share with the Tribunal the material you have in your possession, and I wish you a safe return home again. And as you know, you'll not be alone on your way home. At least the last part, you'll be accompanied by a Tribunal official. You may follow the usher. Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we don't need the witness for this.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just want a clarification. Will we be allowed to meet with the witness once again before he leaves The Hague in order to thank him and to wish him goodbye? Of course, we are not going to speak about anything on the record. That instruction is clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The Prosecution has absolutely no objection to the Defence saying something to the witness afterwards, and I think the instructions have been clear and counsel will abide by them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. As long as you abide by and as long as the witness abides by the instruction that it's just a farewell greeting rather than anything related to the testimony of the witness or the materials which the Chamber made efforts to make available to the parties. Having said this, perhaps it would be best to take the break now before we would invite the Defence to call its next witness and resume at a quarter past 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We're waiting for the witness to be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Gvozden.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before you give evidence, the Rules require that you make a solemn declaration. May I invite you to make that declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
