utterances.text: Mr. Gvozden, you'll first be examined by Mr. Ivetic. Mr. Ivetic is a member of the Mladic Defence team. You may proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Good day, General.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO GVOZDEN
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Could you please state your full name for the record.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO GVOZDEN
utterances.text: My name is Bosko Gvozden. I am a general of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I would like to start today by asking you about 65 ter number 1D1688.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Which I would ask to be called up in e-court. A clean copy of the -- a hard copy of the statement has been given to the usher prior to court. In B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And again, for e-court purposes the 65 ter number is 1D1688.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's just verify whether the witness has received a B/C/S copy or just an English copy, which may not greatly assist him. Mr. Usher, could you please check with the witness whether --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have received a copy in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then we can proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, if we can look at the first page of this document, can you tell us whose signature appears on this page?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO GVOZDEN
utterances.text: This is my signature, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we can now turn to page 9 in the Serbian original, page 10 in the English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, there is a signature under the witness confirmation section with the date 16 June 2014. Whose signature is that?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO GVOZDEN
utterances.text: That is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And after signing this statement in June of this year, did you have occasion to read through the same in the Serbian language with me the other day to confirm if everything is correctly recorded therein?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO GVOZDEN
utterances.text: I had the opportunity to read my statement to confirm that everything in it is accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And do you stand by everything that is written in the statement as being accurately recorded?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO GVOZDEN
utterances.text: I stand by everything that I stated in the statement and it is all accurately recorded in the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, sir, if I were to ask you questions today about the same matters as contained in your written statement, would your answers to those questions be the same in substance as what we find written in your statement?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO GVOZDEN
utterances.text: I could write a novel in answer to each of the questions, but the gist is given in my answers as they are recorded in the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, sir, today you have taken the solemn declaration to tell the truth. Does that mean that the information as contained in your written statement is truthful?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO GVOZDEN
utterances.text: It means that I provided truthful information and as such they have been written accurately in my statement and I myself signed the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would tender the written statement 1D1688 into evidence. There are no associated exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, do you stand by your partly -- your -- your objections on certain parts?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. No further argument.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The Chamber admits into evidence the statement in its entirety. The Prosecution has relied on events in Croatia in 1991 extensively and it is not easy to draw exactly a line where, in the paragraphs 9 to 17, where it is background or where it is responding to elements of the evidence that was adduced by the Prosecution. Therefore, Madam Registrar, the number for the statement in its entirety without redactions would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D1688 receives number D618, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D618 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I have a summary of the evidence in the statement that I'd like to read at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The witness, Bosko Gvozden, is a professional military officer who was commander of the communications regiment at Zagreb when the war started. Later he set up the communications regiment of the VRS and the communications system at Han Pijesak. Then he became commander of the Gradiska Light Infantry Brigade. After the war --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Gradiska.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The Gradiska Light Infantry Brigade. After --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, Witness --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Gradisce is in Austria.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, this is just a summary and is not evidence itself. The evidence is found in your statement, so therefore there is no need. This is just to inform the public. There is no need to make any corrections. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: After the war, he was an assistant to the minister of defence for international military co-operation and head of the international military co-operation administration. He retired from active service in 2004 as a major-general. General Gvozden's statement details in Croatia how the Territorial Defence forces that were supposed to guard his noncombat communications regiment turned their guns on the regiment and blocked and attacked the barracks with the help of Croat paramilitaries. The witness himself spent 60 days imprisoned by these forces. The barracks were subjected to psychological warfare and threat of attack, while the water, electricity, and the communications lines were cut off. Later, as to the VRS, General Gvozden states that the communications system of the VRS was established with only part of the communications equipment that existed at the communications regiment in Sarajevo. Attacks of the Bosnian Muslim forces on the radio relay systems and stations led to personnel being killed and equipment being destroyed. The witness stated that command communications lines were strictly defined and there were no such lines with Belgrade in any form. Of footage of General Mladic speaking from a phone at the VMA in Belgrade, General Gvozden says at that time General Mladic was only able to use a regular phone, the equivalent of speaking through a megaphone, and it was not possible to perform command tasks over the same. Communications is one thing and commanding another, different lines are used. As to General Mladic, the witness never heard in person or through the means of commanding, and he had access to encrypted documents, nor did he see any order that would imply liquidation [Realtime transcript read in error "liberation"] of civilians, individuals hors de combat, or mistreatment or torture of captured enemy soldiers. This is best reflected in General Mladic's comportment -- this is best reflected in General Mladic's comportment towards the captured enemy soldiers and in his willingness to do whatever it takes to have our captured soldiers released. It is incompatible with his personality that he could order the killings in Srebrenica. This completes the summary of the witness's statement. I'm told that page 65, line 20, has "liberation" instead of "liquidation." If I misspoke, I apologise. The term should be "liquidation."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This has been corrected now. You've finished your summary?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then if you have any questions for the witness, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: General Gvozden, I have a few questions for you. First of all, I would like to look at paragraph 35 of your statement found on page 7 in both languages.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO GVOZDEN
utterances.text: I see it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: When you say here at least a basic encryption method must be in place, what do you mean? What are some of the basic encryption methods?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO GVOZDEN
utterances.text: When one trains people in the most basic soldierly duties up to the most complex, the highest functions in the army, we would always explain and train people and make sure that everybody knew that in command it is obligatory to encrypt documents that are being used. The only permissible, open conversations that are unencrypted are in the middle of battle, when encryption would cause casualties and defeat; for example, in mechanised and armoured units where unencrypted conversations are permitted in open lines during combat. But it's not otherwise possible to encounter a trained professional soldier who doesn't know this, particularly who, in a dirty war that we went through, would not heed these rules. What we have seen, what I have managed to see in this footage, where --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm going to object.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- unprotected, unsecured conversations can be seen --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It was a simple question asking for methods of encryption. He has not even gotten close to answering the question and is just going off.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Am I to respond? Is there an objection to the question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, I think it is an objection against letting the witness expound on matters which are not asked. I think that's what Mr. McCloskey wants to emphasize.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Could you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But, Mr. Ivetic, do you consider what the witness tells us to be an explanation of basic encryption methods?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I asked him to explain what he meant by a basic method of encryption must be in place and to describe encryption methods. I believe he is dealing in part with my question and has now moved on to paragraph 36 which was not yet a part of my --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: -- question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think that you indeed asked for an explanation as to "must be in place," and I think the witness is explaining that to some extent. Perhaps next time it would be better not to put two questions in one line but take them one by one, Mr. Ivetic. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, could tell us what are some of the basic encryption methods that you had in mind?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO GVOZDEN
utterances.text: I can be quite brief. Other than in direct combat, there are basic encryption methods. They can be manual or machine encryption methods. For the transfer of information between commands, one would use automatic devices that are used for the encryption of total communications between two communication nodes. Then for individual communications, there is manual encryption of a specific document.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness is kindly asked to speak more slowly. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please speak more slowly for the interpreters. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: General Gvozden, could you tell us the difference between a line used for communication purposes and one used for command purposes?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO GVOZDEN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Command lines are strictly established in all armies of the world, including ours. They follow the existing hierarchy. The Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska, the commander at the head of the staff, then you would have the subordinate units, the corps, the independent brigades, the regiments, that would be subordinated. That would be the line of command. All other lines have different names, such as co-ordination, reporting, calling in or alerting, different professional things. These communications are key in command duties. We refer to them as command lines, and they are of particular importance, both in the organisational and in the technical sense, and these lines are secured by encryption. So commanders at all levels all the way up to the commander of the Main Staff are obliged to use that system of communications when they are communicating. For just regular communication they can use any system at -- then it was called PTT. Now it's called mobile communications or similar.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, in answer to one of my prior questions, you started talking about footage you've seen and I presume you mean the footage referenced in paragraph 36 of your statement. Could you just briefly finish your comments as to the footage that is described in paragraph 36 of your statement?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO GVOZDEN
utterances.text: I looked at the footage and I saw General Mladic in a relaxed situation, evidently among friends, aware that he was being filmed by a camera. This is perhaps footage that people would want to keep in their personal archive. And it was my conclusion that he allowed himself to be filmed and that he wanted to show how the commander of the Main Staff could communicate with his men. Perhaps he was talking to a colleague who was in the next room. So perhaps it was a little bit of self-promotion because it's a handsome, charming man, women adored him, so perhaps he just used that opportunity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, rather than hearing the interpretation of this witness on whether he was communicating with someone in the next-door room, if you present paragraph 36, it certainly would assist the Chamber to know what the witness looked at. So as to he has comments on video which is not defined, then we would not know whether it's in evidence or whether -- you understand what I mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: To fully understand the testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, it is my understanding that there is one recording of General Mladic at the VMA and it's P --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, if you -- if it is in evidence. It is in evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It is in evidence, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Number?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: P1147, the Srebrenica trial video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. And that is --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And it is -- it is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. I would have expected this to be identified so that it is on the record as well at what the witness looked at. Not only for us to know that it is this but also it to be clear. Please proceed. We now do understand that witness looked at P1147.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: But the Srebrenica trial video is a very long trial video. Perhaps you can, now or later, indicate where the witness saw Mr. Mladic in this video.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I can. It is the third segment of that group of videos, the video with an identifier number V000-9267-1-A, with the time stamp beginning at 00:49:24 going to 00:51:39.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can look at paragraph 32 of your statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That is on the previous page in the English and also the Serbian. And it bleeds over into the next page in both. Or at least in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Here you say that reserve officers had to replace professional officers at some of the radio relays. What can you tell us about these reserve officers in terms of their training and skills in the field of radio communications?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO GVOZDEN
utterances.text: To put it most briefly, it was a moment of major changes in the whole unit, in the whole army. Some people were preparing to leave Bosnia-Herzegovina by 19 May 1992, and those who were to stay had to take up their places, the places of those who were leaving. Therefore, there was a shortage of experts in communications, where trained, qualified people are necessary, so we recruited lot of people from the then PTT, now called Telekom. They were great masters in their profession. So we somehow managed to get over this moment of upheaval in the process of establishing the army. Just one more thing. These people were mostly engineers of telecommunications, technicians, people of that kind of profile.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, sir, for both the professional and the reserve officers, could one be assigned to work with the communications equipment without having a prior training and speciality in communications?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO GVOZDEN
utterances.text: No, no. Recruits were selected and later soldiers and specialists for the units that we later formed, such as the communications regiment, which was the most capable and the best trained, the one catering to the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska, and they were responsible for the entire communications system in the military and technical sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, for the remainder of this paragraph you highlight some of the main problems; namely, attacks by the Army of BiH on radio relay stations which led to killed personnel and destroyed equipment. How often were such attacks by the enemy forces undertaken on radio relay stations of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO GVOZDEN
utterances.text: Radio relay hubs and separate radio relay stations are the most delicate links in the communications system. Everybody in the profession knows it, and the enemy also knows it. It is the weakest link that needs to be destroyed in order to damage the system of command. It is the same handwriting, so to speak, that I experienced in Croatia. Having survived that, I had experience and I knew what I could expect, so I knew very clearly in Bosnia-Herzegovina which way it would go. However, time was short. The units of the Territorial Defence around the communications hub that were trained and equipped to guard it and the crews who were inside the hubs working on 24-hour shifts could not change the population around them from a hostile to a friendly one. So it was constantly open to abuse. The Muslim population, although not everywhere, just those who were really bent on fighting, attacked the communications centres, trying to destroy the command system and thus undermine the leadership that had already started to work. It was very intense. At one point, even the main communications centre located on Veliki Zep mountain was attacked. It was right next to the Main Staff. They took advantage of a moment when the crew was very busy. They knew the schedule of their work and their roster. And they managed to capture part of the crew at Veliki Zep. We dealt with it later, but the people who were responsible for this attack were not liquidated. They were later exchanged.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'd like to move to paragraph 34 of your statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: On page 7 in both languages.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, sir, there you state in February of 1993 you became commander of a light infantry brigade. Your previous positions were as a communications officer in noncombat formations. Can you explain for us what experience and knowledge you had that allowed you to take over command of a combat unit; namely, the Gradiska Light Infantry Brigade?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO GVOZDEN
utterances.text: The pronunciation is Gradiska. Gradisce is in Austria. There are at least three reasons why I opted to become a general-type commander and accepted the post of the commander of the light infantry brigade and later Tactical Group 6. First of all, I started my career in the armoured brigade in Banja Luka. First I was communications specialist and then communications commander. There was the competitive spirit. I learned to shoot, to drive, and later at the command I planned drills of the armoured battalion, and I got a feeling for the deployment, disposition of units in battle, and I believe myself capable to take up this job. In terms of education, I finished the two-year staff academy. And a second reason is that the skeleton of the communications regiment was already established, not by me alone but together with others. The bulk of the job had been completed by that time. And the third reason, as the English say, last but not least, I had experience from Croatia which confirmed that the decisions I made in some key moments, decisions in the field of general military command were correct and I had not learned them in theory and I had not had prior experience. Let me mention just my main, principal decision. While I was surrounded at the barracks in Samobor, I received a direction from the then General Staff of the Yugoslav People's Army, that I simply couldn't believe. I couldn't believe my eyes reading the task. The task was to breakout of the encirclement with the forces we had, with what I had in the communications regiment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, is there any challenge to the witness being fit to take over combat position or any -- his competence in that respect?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I don't know, Mr. President. But it's not something I'm interested in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We have now listened for three or four minutes to the reasons why the witness thought that he could accept such a position. Mr. Ivetic, unless you can explain to us what the relevance of it is, we can move on. There seems to be no challenge to the fitness of this witness to take up such a position.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We can move on then, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'd like to move to General Mladic whom you discuss at paragraphs 41 and thereafter --

utterances.speaker: BOSKO GVOZDEN
utterances.text: Just one more thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, please listen to the question that Mr. Ivetic will put to you and answer that question. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can move on to General Mladic whom you discuss at paragraphs 41 and beyond on pages 8 through 9 of your statement, what was General Mladic's reputation amongst yourself and other professional officers stemming from his activities before he assumed command of the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO GVOZDEN
utterances.text: I first heard of the General from the regular reports and the information that circulated in the army, then from my close friend, regrettably now late General Lisica, who was then a colonel, a chief of the armoured units in the Knin corps, whereas General Mladic was the commander of the Knin corps. He was a man I knew very well and whom I believed, and from General Lisica I heard only all the best about General Lisica [as interpreted] who described him as a witty Herzegovina man who was dealing with very difficult problems in those difficult times of war. His fame spread by word of mouth. You know that word of mouth is the greatest medium, stronger than all the mass media. So everybody knew by that time that a new commander has appeared on the scene, somebody to respect as a leader. That was the image I had of General Mladic even before meeting him.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, General Gvozden, as a lifelong professionally trained military officer, what is your appraisal of General Mladic's orders while commanding the VRS Main Staff from the standpoint of military legitimacy and correctness?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO GVOZDEN
utterances.text: By the nature of my job, I had access to all the documents sent from the Main Staff to subordinate units, and my duties included monitoring the lines of command into all the directions including written documents. I controlled encryption, et cetera. There is not a single document that I had seen, not even in preparation, nor any official documents, where you could even remotely find anything that deviated from international conventions or the laws governing the army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, I'm looking at the clock. You have used 35 minutes until now of which four or five minutes on a matter where I had to stop the witness because it turned out to be rather irrelevant. Could you please seek to conclude your examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I will, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: General, what can you tell us in closing as your appraisal of the character and professionalism of General Ratko Mladic?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO GVOZDEN
utterances.text: I met General Ratko Mladic for the first time when the Main Staff of the VRS was formed in Han Pijesak, the place where the Main Staff had its headquarters. I met him and General Milovanovic who was his deputy, Chief of the Main Staff. What I saw just confirmed what I had heard about that man before, that he was a very witty, quick-spirited man, very friendly, affectionate man, but very, very strict. And I knew based on my experience of combat that that is the primary requirement, the first condition for the mission to be accomplished with the smallest possible losses. I appreciated that quality in him and I was not alone. Everybody appreciated it. His soldiers also had great respect for him because he never set out battles in his own office or in the offices of his subordinate commanders. He was always on the forward line together with the fighting men. That reputation spread even without internet, and the people held him in high esteem for that. Now, when I was preparing to come here to testify, I met with a lot of people who told me, "Please, pass on our greetings to that great man, our general." I can't change the facts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're supposed not to enter into any greeting ceremonies, so you've -- anything else you would like to add to your answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I think that sentence that I did not have time to finish is important for the Court. The one I meant to say, that he -- that I couldn't believe the order that told me I had to break out of the barracks, break out of the encirclement with my own forces. That commander made a decision on the breakout involving huge losses, and nobody was considering it or condemning it; whereas the guilt, the responsibility of the command in those circumstances is great.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Since you have mentioned it, I do have to ask now, you have said "that commander" and "the command" that did make a decision on the breakout. What commander are you speaking of?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO GVOZDEN
utterances.text: I'm talking about the commander of the 28th Division of the so-called BH Army in Srebrenica. I know the commander had run away, but the command or somebody in the command made that decision to breakout and that was a mistake.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm going to stop you again. First of all, the witness was interrupted when he dwelled away from the question, and he now says, "I want to add anything," which is not in response to your question. So therefore, Mr. Ivetic, was it your last question? Because we do not need to elaborate on matters the witness raised without being asked about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That was my last question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That was your last question. Then thank you very much for that. Mr. Gvozden, you'll now be cross-examined by Mr. McCloskey. You'll find Mr. McCloskey to your right. And Mr. McCloskey is counsel for the Prosecution. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President, Your Honours, everyone. Mr. President, I see I have no questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Ivetic, I -- then the questions in cross-examination could not have triggered any need for further examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But your hope must be with my colleagues and with myself. I have no questions. The Bench has no questions. Therefore --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If I could just thank the witness for coming on behalf of the Defence. That's all I wanted -- raised to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, not only on behalf of the Defence but as you know --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, thank you too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I see what I believe is a -- is just a -- is just a translation on paragraph 21 of the statement. And if we could go into private session briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session. We need the witness for it, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Most likely, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Very possibly, but I doubt it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, let's then --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It -- you'll -- it might --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One -- one second.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Madam Registrar. We should have turned into open session earlier because the very short issue raised in private session was followed, and that should have been in open session, by establishing that the evidence of the witness, the examination, had been concluded. The Chamber has thanked the witness for coming to The Hague and wished him a safe return home, and we are now at a point to adjourn for the day. Is the Defence tomorrow ready to call its next witness? Yes. Then we adjourn for the day and we resume tomorrow, Thursday, the 4th of September, in this same courtroom, II, at 9.30 in the morning.
